post.description:
Begin registration. **The same 202 for every well-formed request.**

What it used to do — 409 on a duplicate — was a free membership-checking API for anyone
who found the URL. `DESIGN_open_registration.md` §2.

Consume a verification link, verifying the address and possibly approving.

**Failures name their reason.** The token is a secret rather than an identifier, so there
is nothing to enumerate by being precise — and `expired` is what lets the UI offer a
resend instead of a dead end.

Re-issue a verification link. **Answers identically for every address.**

An unknown address, an already-verified one, and a genuinely unverified one all get the
same 202. Anything else makes this the enumeration oracle `register` was changed to stop
being.
Authenticate with email + password. Returns session token on success.
Invalidate the current session. Requires a valid bearer token.

get.description:
List characters, filtered by element, weapon type, rarity or name substring.

**`include_beta` defaults to false, and that default is the feature.** Characters the
manifest names as unreleased are seeded and marked rather than withheld (owner, 2026-09-07)
so `/planner` can price an upcoming one. Every other caller keeps the old list without
changing a line — and because the build editor never lists them, a beta character cannot
reach a build and so cannot reach the optimizer, which is the exclusion that was asked for.

One character with its talents, constellations and ascension passives.

The path parameter is a **string**: 28 of the 150 characters are keyed `10000005-2` …
`10000005-8`, and they are **14 Traveler variants plus 14 practice mannequins**
(`10000117`/`10000118` are Manekin and Manekina, not Traveler bodies). Typing it as an int
would 422 on all of them.

List weapons, filtered by type, rarity or name substring.

**`include_beta` defaults to false**, the twin of the character list's. Only `/planner`
asks, so the build editor never offers a beta weapon and no build can hold one.

It does **not** reach the eight rows carrying an unshipped weapon class: those are a
different exclusion and no flag turns them on.

The caller's own weapons — **equipped first**, then by refinement and level.

Distinct from `/weapons`, which is the 260-row catalogue of every weapon in the game. This
is what you have, and until now nothing published it: a GOOD export lists 320 weapons and
the importer used 68 of them to set `builds.weapon_id`, discarding the rest.

Equipped-first is the **default order rather than a sort option**, because it answers
"what am I actually using" without the user having to ask.

One weapon with its refinement rows and growth curves.

A row whose class the game has not shipped answers 404 like a row that is not there. The
list hides these eight because their **names** are datamine-only (`services/unreleased.py`,
#271), and a detail route that still serves the name on request publishes exactly what
hiding the list was for — a guessable id is not a meaningful barrier.
List artifact sets with their bonus affixes, and whether gcsim can simulate each.
One artifact set with its affixes.

List enemy profiles.

The stats in each row are **curve bases**, not level-90 numbers; `stat_curves` names
the curve each one grows on. See `EnemyProfileRead`.

One enemy profile by row id.

By row id, not `nanoka_id`, because `nanoka_id` is **nullable**: a hand-authored
profile — a test dummy, a crossval target — is a legitimate row that no importer owns
and would be unreachable through a source-keyed route.

What KeqingMains lists as this character's weapons, in the order KQM lists them.

**404 when no guide has been captured**, which is not the same as "KQM recommends nothing" —
a caller showing an empty panel for an uncaptured character would be making a claim about
KQM that nobody made.

Static and committed, never a live fetch: a guide is somebody else's page and it changes.
`scripts/capture_kqm_weapons.py` re-captures deliberately, and the diff is the review.

**The snapshot holds the game's ids and this resolves them here.** It held *row* ids until
2026-09-04, which meant it only worked against the one database it was captured from —
zero of them existed in production, so every recommendation silently missed and both
pickers looked like pickers with no guide. Resolving at read time keeps the published
`weapon_id` a row id, so no client had to change.

Declared **above** `/characters/{nanoka_id}` is unnecessary — the paths differ by a
segment — but it is declared beside it so the two are read together.

The seven visions and their emblems, in the order the game lists them.

A filter bar needs both. Served rather than restated so the client never builds an icon
basename out of an element name — `app/services/element_symbols.py` explains at length why
that string is an allowlist and not an f-string.

Unauthenticated like the rest of the catalogue: it describes the game, not the caller.

get.description: The caller's artifacts, in game slot order — flower, plume, sands, goblet, circlet.

The caller's whole inventory at one instant, for the client-side search.

Answers `304` when the caller already holds this version. See `InventorySnapshot` for
why the browser holds it at all (OQ-S3).

Every tier of every set the caller owns a piece of, in kernel terms.

**Why this exists rather than reusing `/builds/{id}/search-context`.** That endpoint
already returns these, but it requires a *hit* — and the rotation objective has none: it
scores a whole gcsim run, not one Cutting DMG. Passing a hit purely to reach the bonuses
would couple the rotation path to the single-hit path's requirements.

**Why not derived in the browser.** `/artifact-sets` already publishes each affix's
`add_props`, so a client could translate them itself — and would then own a second copy of
the `FIGHT_PROP_*` → kernel-quantity mapping. `OptimizeService` says why that is refused:
the mapping decides what every stat means, and O.1/O.2 exist so it happens once, here.

**Only static `add_props` become stats**, the same rule `artifact_optimizer` documents: a
conditional bonus has `FIGHT_PROP_NONE` for every prop and its numbers live in
`param_list`. Nine of the sixty 2-piece affixes at 7.0.51 are conditional, six of them
ability-scoped DMG bonuses a flat stat pool cannot express. They arrive here with empty
`stats`, and a caller that means to score them has to say so — `TASKS_optimizer_reach.md`
B.2 and B.3.

Asked as a set question rather than by reading the inventory, for the reason
`owned_sets` gives: `search`'s cap would silently omit a set from a large account, and a
ranking missing an option looks exactly like a ranking.

get.description:
The vocabulary an inventory needs to draw a row.

A.3. `slot` and `main_stat_type` carry the source's internal spellings — `equip_bracer`,
`FIGHT_PROP_HP_PERCENT` — which are keys, not labels. And the stored values are
units-dependent: `4780.0` for flat HP, `0.466` for HP%. A page with neither fact prints
"0.466 HP%" or "478000% HP", and neither looks obviously wrong at a glance.

Published **once** rather than decorated onto every row: 26 stats and 5 slots repeated
across 800 pieces is the same table 800 times.

Declared above `/{artifact_id}` — FastAPI matches in declaration order, and below it this
is an artifact whose id is the word "options", which 404s and looks like an empty
inventory rather than a routing mistake.

post.description:
Import a GOOD export into the caller's inventory.

`mode` is required — see `GoodImportRequest`. A malformed *envelope* is a 400, because
the file is not a GOOD export at all and nothing about it can be salvaged. A malformed
*artifact* is not: it lands in `rejected` and the rest of the inventory imports, because
someone with 800 artifacts and two odd ones wants the 798.

A `replace` that resolved **nothing** is a 409 and deletes nothing — see
`ReplaceRefusedError`.

get.description: One of the caller's artifacts.

patch.description:
Attach a piece to a build, or take it off.

A.1. `Artifact.build_id` has existed since Chunk C and nothing set it, so an imported
inventory could not be attached to anything.

**A filled slot is refused, naming the piece that holds it** (OQ-A2). Swapping is a
reasonable thing to want and a terrible thing to do unasked: the displaced piece is still
equipped in the user's head, and they would find out later, from a damage number.
`uq_artifacts_build_slot` would otherwise make this a 500 — the shape
`uq_builds_owner_character` had before T.1a.

delete.description:
Delete one of the caller's artifacts.

404 rather than 403 for a piece owned by someone else: the repository is scoped, so a
foreign id is indistinguishable from a missing one here — and telling a caller which of
the two it was would confirm that some other user owns that id.

put.description:
Set the owner's build ranking, best first.

`BACKLOG_frontend.md` §3. The ranking answers "who gets the piece" when two builds want
the same artifact — see the optimizer's equip path, which until now refused outright.

**Declared before `/{build_id}` on purpose.** FastAPI matches in declaration order, so a
literal path registered after a parameterised one is unreachable: `/priority` would arrive
as `build_id="priority"` and 404 as a missing build. That is a silent routing bug, not an
error, which is why it is stated here rather than left to path order to imply.

get.description:
The talent keys a build may carry, and the level cap.

Declared **above** `/{build_id}` — FastAPI matches in declaration order, and below it this
path is a build whose id is the word "options", which 404s and looks like an empty form
rather than a routing mistake. Same trap R.5 met.

No database, no owner: this is the vocabulary, not the caller's data. It still requires a
bearer token, because everything under `/builds` does and an exception would be a hole
someone has to remember.
One of the caller's builds, with the catalogue rows a page draws it from.

patch.description:
Partially update one of the caller's builds.

The pairing is re-checked against the **merged** result, not against the patch body. What
is being validated is character-and-weapon *together*, and a patch that moves a sword
build onto an archer names only fields that are individually fine while leaving the
stored weapon unwieldable.

delete.description: Delete one of the caller's builds. Its artifacts are unequipped, not deleted.

get.description:
Every hit this build can be asked about, at its own talent levels.

M.2. What `HitSpec.talent` will accept, from the same parse that resolves it — so a page
offering these cannot name one the resolver refuses.

A talent the build has no level for is **absent rather than offered**: offering it would
produce a refusal the moment it was picked. A build with no character returns nothing,
which is the truthful answer rather than a 404 about a build that exists.

post.description:
Everything the browser kernel needs to search, except the inventory.

O.1. `frontend/src/app/sim/search.ts` has been a working optimizer that nothing could
reach, because `SearchContext` needs a hit and a base — and the base is keyed by **kernel
quantity** while the API speaks `FIGHT_PROP_*`. That mapping is
`stat_calculator._quantity_for_prop`; it decides what every stat means and refuses rather
than guessing, so a TypeScript copy of it would be a second definition of the vocabulary
with a silent failure mode.

Takes the same body as `/explain` deliberately: a caller asking "what should I wear for
this hit" and one asking "why does this score what it does" are describing the same hit,
and two request shapes for one description is how they drift apart.

The inventory is **not** here. `/artifacts/inventory` carries it, ETag'd, because the
browser holds it across searches and revalidates cheaply (OQ-S3).

Why this build scores what it scores — and, by default, why it beats what is worn.

Every number here **arrives** rather than being computed: contributions come from
`build_combination_log`, the same path the search and the ranker use; set text comes from
the catalogue verbatim; the simulation figure comes from `sim_retrieval` carrying its own
measured divergence. Nothing in the explanation layer multiplies anything, because a
second implementation of the chain would be free to disagree with the first (DESIGN §1
A6).

Score each candidate weapon in this build, holding the artifacts fixed.

**Two limits are reported rather than buried, because both can change the answer and not
merely its precision:**

- **Weapon passives are not applied here.** They are imported into `weapon_refinements`,
  and 242 of 260 weapons carry one while 5 are expressible in this chain — so the gap is
  frequently the entire reason to equip a weapon. `unmodelled_passives` names every
  candidate that has a passive and the response's `caveat` says the ordering may be wrong.
  **`POST /compare-weapons/gcsim` is the tier that does apply them** (W.6): it costs
  minutes rather than milliseconds, so this endpoint stays rather than being replaced.
- **Artifacts are held fixed.** DESIGN §3.5's fuller version searches per weapon and
  compares the winners, but searches belong on the client. This answers "which weapon is
  better in the build I have", which is a cheaper and different question — a weapon
  wanting a different artifact set loses a comparison it would win with its own pieces.

The gcsim configs for a weapon comparison — one per candidate (W.6).

**This is the tier that knows weapon passives.** `POST /compare-weapons` ranks on base ATK
and the substat and reports `unmodelled_passives`, which is not a precision caveat: 242 of
260 weapons carry a passive and 5 are expressible in the Chunk F chain, so a stat-stick can
outrank the weapon whose passive is the entire reason to equip it. gcsim implements them.

**The server emits configs and does not simulate.** `RESEARCH_gcsim_embed.md` §6 put gcsim
in the browser, and W.4 measured a full sword pool at ~96 s across four workers — a job on
the user's machine, not a request a server holds open. The browser runs these through
`sim/gcsim.ts` and ranks them with `sim/weapon-ranking.ts`, which reports which pairs the
run could **not** separate.

**A candidate gcsim cannot key is refused by name, never dropped.** A silently omitted
candidate produces a ranking missing a weapon the user asked about, and the omission is
invisible because the result still looks like a complete answer.

The two gcsim configs a damage recipe is built from (R.3).

**The server emits; the browser runs.** `RESEARCH_gcsim_embed.md` §6 put gcsim in the
browser, and a calibration is ~3.2 s of work per set — a job on the user's machine, not a
request a server holds open.

**One calibration per 4-piece state.** Every 4-piece bonus in the game is conditional
(`RESEARCH_conditional_sets.md`), so only a run with the set equipped can hold it, and R.2
measured the cost of not doing so at **15–25 % understated**. A five-slot combination
reaches at most one 4-piece, which is what keeps this `S + 1` rather than a product.

**The probe moves exactly one stat.** `resolveConversions` identifies what a frozen term
converts from by comparing the two runs; a probe that moved two stats by the same factor
could not separate them, and the recipe would rather report a conversion unresolved than
guess between them.

get.description:
The build's equipped artifacts, summed in the kernel's quantities.

What `/calculate` needs to evaluate a calibrated recipe at a build's *real* gear — the
recipe is calibrated at a reference set of stats, and this is what replaces them.

Deliberately not part of `/artifacts/inventory`: that payload is fetched across a whole
inventory, and a field added to it is paid for once per artifact. This answers a question
about five.

This user's saved runs, newest first.

**Never ordered by score.** A score is a damage number for one character against one
enemy, so ranking two runs for different characters by it would invent a comparison the
data does not support.

A published run by its key, readable without owning it.

A private run **404s rather than 403s**: telling a caller that a key exists but is not
theirs is telling them the key is worth guessing at.
One of the caller's own runs, in full.

Rename a run, or publish it.

**The result is not editable.** A saved run records what happened, and letting it be
rewritten would make the library a place where numbers are asserted rather than measured.

get.description: The caller's rotations, optionally just one team's.

post.description: Save a rotation, having checked every step against its team.

get.description:
What an editor may offer: the ten actions, and the caller's teams with their rosters.

Declared **above** `/{rotation_id}` — FastAPI matches in declaration order, and below it
this path would be swallowed as a rotation whose id is the word "options".

One request rather than a walk from team to four builds to four characters. That walk
would also have to map `character_id` (a UUID) to the `nanoka_id` a step names, which is
a conversion the client has no business performing.

post.description:
Read a gcsim config back into rotation steps, or refuse and say why.

**This creates nothing.** The steps come back as a preview and are saved, if at all,
through the ordinary create endpoint — see `RotationImportRead` on why.

A config this app emitted round-trips exactly. Anything else is refused with **422 naming
every line** it could not express, rather than imported without them. gcsim's language is
far larger than a list of `(character, action, repeat)`: conditional guards on energy or
status, `wait` for buff alignment, loops that are not `while 1`. Dropping an
`if .noelle.energy > 40` would leave a rotation that looks like the author's, carries
their name, and simulates to a number they never published — and the user would have no
way to see the difference. `rotation_parser` is written at length about this.

Parse and check rotation source, without saving anything.

**This is what makes the source view possible at all**, and it is deliberately the *same*
parser and the same validator the importer runs. The owner's ruling of 2026-09-03 allows
a typed surface where buttons cannot reach; `DECISIONS.md` §32 records why that is not a
second vocabulary, and the reason is exactly this endpoint: text typed in the editor goes
through the code an imported config goes through, so nothing authored can escape the rules
an import obeys.

**It never refuses.** Unparseable source still returns a tree — one `raw` node holding it —
because the editor sends this on every keystroke and half-typed text is the normal state,
not an error. What is wrong with it comes back in `diagnostics` with positions to underline.

The same import, from a gcsim database link rather than its pasted config.

**This is a fetch, not a simulation.** One GET of a stored document per import, and what
comes back is saved here as steps — so nothing depends on gcsim once this returns. That
matters because the owner's standing ruling is that this project does not push compute to
them.

**The endpoint it reads is undocumented**: `/api/share/db/<id>` is the route gcsim's own
single-page app calls, read out of its published bundle, and it may change. Survivable
because the import is a one-time write — a break costs new imports and never saved ones,
and the paste box beside it is the fallback. `gcsim_share` says the rest, including why
this takes an id and never a URL.

Compile steps that have not been saved, so an editor can show what it is building.

Declared **above** `/{rotation_id}` for the reason `/options` and `/library` are: FastAPI
matches in declaration order, and below it this is a rotation whose id is "preview".

Writes nothing. It is a POST because the steps are a body, not because it changes anything
— and it is rate-limited like a write because it does real work per call.

The same validation as a save, deliberately: a preview that accepted a step the save would
refuse is a preview of a rotation that cannot exist.

schema.title: Response Preview Compile Api V1 Rotations Preview Post

get.description:
Published rotations, from every user on this instance.

Declared **above** `/{rotation_id}` for the reason `/options` is: FastAPI matches in
declaration order, and below it this path would be swallowed as a rotation whose id is the
word "library".

`characters` matches a rotation whose character set is **exactly** these ids — not a
superset. `DESIGN_rotation_library.md` §3 calls this filter one that "claims nothing", and
that is only true if it means what it says: a four-character rotation surfacing for a
three-character query would be a recommendation wearing a filter's clothes.

Three queries for the page, not three per row: the rotations, their character sets, and
their like counts. A per-row lookup is the shape that turns a twenty-row page into
sixty-one round trips and looks fine until the page grows.

post.description:
Mark a published rotation useful. Idempotent — liking twice is a no-op.

**Liking your own is allowed.** It costs nothing to permit, and a rule against it is a rule
to explain, enforce and test for no benefit anyone asked for.

delete.description: Take a like back. Also idempotent: un-liking what you never liked is not an error.

post.description:
Copy a published rotation onto one of the caller's own teams.

A shared rotation belongs to its author's team, so copying it means **re-resolving every
step against the caller's**. A step naming a character their team does not field is
**refused, naming the character** — never dropped and never substituted, which is the rule
`app/models/rotation.py` (OQ-R2) already applies to a rotation gone stale.

The copy is private, whatever the original was: publishing is something a user does.

get.description: One rotation.

patch.description:
Rename a rotation, replace its steps, or publish it.

Steps are replaced wholesale rather than patched per index. A rotation is an ordered
list, so "change step 3" and "insert before step 3" are the same edit to the client and
a different one to a per-index API — and the ambiguity would land on whoever wrote the UI.

**Publishing is `visibility`, not a `/publish` route** (L.2). A separate endpoint would be
a second way to write one column, needing the same ownership check written twice — and this
one is already here, in `_require` against the owner-scoped repository, which answers 404
rather than 403 to a stranger and so does not confirm the row exists.

post.description:
The gcsim action list this rotation becomes.

Offered because a compiler nobody can inspect is a compiler nobody can check, and the
complaint that started this chunk was about a syntax that hides what it is doing.

A rotation whose team has since lost a character compiles to a **422 naming every
offending step** — see `rotation_compiler`. It is not repaired here, and the steps are
left exactly as authored.

schema.title: Response Compile To Gcsim Api V1 Rotations  Rotation Id  Compile Post

post.description:
The cache key identifying "this build, running this rotation, against this target".

R.6. `context_key` decides whether a cached gcsim run answers the question being asked,
and getting it wrong is not a performance bug — it serves a confident number computed for
something else. **So the server computes it.** Before this, the only callers were tests,
and a client wanting a cached run had to reproduce a canonicalising SHA-256 by hand; the
second implementation would have drifted, and the drift would look like a cache hit.

The rotation is fed in through `rotation_signature`, which shares `_resolve` with the
compiler — so the key and the config gcsim actually receives cannot disagree about who a
step names. The target comes through `gcsim_config.target_fields`, for the same reason.

get.description:
Every character that can be owned, with this user's answer where they have given one.

**The catalogue left-joined to the roster**, rather than the roster alone: the tab has to
offer a toggle for a character the user has never touched, and a row that does not exist
cannot carry one.

**Two exclusions, for two different reasons.** Mannequins are never characters and go by
nanoka id prefix; the unreleased Traveler bodies will be characters and go by carrying a
weapon class the game has not shipped. `services/roster.py` and `services/unreleased.py`
argue them separately.

**The second was by talent count on this branch and is by weapon class now**, because #271
landed the same exclusion for a stronger reason while this was open: `WEAPON_CROSSBOW` also
carries eight unreleased *weapon* names, so hiding the class hides a leak the talent-count
rule never touched. Both rules select the same two Traveler rows at nanoka 7.0.51.

**This route reads `select(Character)` directly**, not `CharacterRepository`, so it does
not inherit the catalogue's exclusions and has to state them — which is how the mannequin
rule already came to be written out here twice.

Ordered by `display_name`, not `name` — sixteen rows sharing one `name` have no order
among themselves under the latter, so the Travelers appeared in whatever order the database
returned and could shuffle between requests.

patch.description:
Record the user's own answer about one character.

Always written as `manual`, which is what stops the next import overwriting it. A user who
un-owns a character they have gear for means it; an import that undid that every rescan
would read as the app ignoring them.

get.description:
Every furnishing set, ranked by how much of it this user can still claim.

**Ordered by remaining owned favourites**, which is the same order the owner's
"remaining primogems" would give: the reward is one constant per character, and a positive
constant multiplier cannot change a ranking.

put.description:
Record that this character has been invited to this set.

**Per character per set**, because that is how the reward is given: a set favoured by three
characters you own is worth three invitations and 60 primogems. Ticking the set as a whole
would either lose the two you had not done or ask you to repeat the one you had.

Idempotent — ticking twice is not an error, and a client retrying a request it is not sure
landed should not have to care.

delete.description:
Un-tick one character on one set.

**The reason a completed character stays on the row rather than vanishing**: a user has to
be able to undo a tick, which means they have to be able to see it.

put.description:
Record that this set has been built.

**Separate from the invitations, because it is separate work.** Owner, 2026-09-03:
*"it takes time and effort to build them so that's different from the invites."* A set can
be built with nobody invited yet, and every character can be invited to a set the user
never told us they built — neither implies the other.

Idempotent, like the invitation endpoints.

delete.description: Un-mark a set as built — a set can be dismantled, and a tick can be a mistake.

get.description:
Which ER buckets this context already has at the server's pin.

The browser asks this **first**, and simulates only the gap. A cold context answers with
an empty list rather than a 404: "nothing cached yet" is the ordinary state of a corpus
that fills on demand, and it is not an error to be in it.

post.description:
Cache a run the browser finished.

The pin is a query parameter rather than a body field so that a client which omits it
gets a 422 naming it, instead of a body validated against a default nobody chose.

get.description:
The cached run for a build at this ER — **or a stated reason there is none**.

Always 200. `retrieved` is either present or explicitly null with `not_retrieved_because`
beside it, and never a distant neighbour dressed up as a close one. See
`RetrievalOutcome` for why "nothing close enough is cached" is an answer rather than a
404: an error invites a retry or a swallowed exception, and the second is the silent
fallback DESIGN §3.5 forbids by name.

One cached run, or a 404 that says which bucket was missing.

The 404 is the outcome D.3 turns into a stated one: a caller that gets it must simulate
or say so, and must never widen its search to a neighbouring bucket and report the score
as though it were this one's.
What a plan can be built from, optionally narrowed to one character's talents.

post.description: Price a plan. Writes nothing.

get.description: This caller's stock, zero-filled across the whole catalogue.

patch.description:
Correct the stock a bill is priced against.

**A later GOOD import replaces every row written here**, deliberately —
`docs/DESIGN_planner_materials.md` §2 argues it and an integration test pins it. The
surface says so; this is the route that makes it true.

post.description:
Return the odds of each goal in the plan, on one shared budget.

Milestones are **cumulative**: a rung's chance is the chance of reaching it *and*
everything before it. That is the whole difference from asking about each banner
separately, where both answers silently assume they own the entire wallet.

get.description:
Return wish income per game version, at the three spending tiers.

Served from `wish_income`, which `scripts/refresh_wish_income.py` fills on a timer. This
route never reaches the workbook: `app/` has one request-time fetch and a third-party
spreadsheet on the request path would be a second.

An empty store is **not** an error — it means the refresher has not run yet, and a page
can say so. Inventing numbers to fill it would be worse.

Banners newest first, paged.

**Paged rather than capped.** `CLAUDE.md` records the planner's materials tab being
"fixed" by truncating a 514-row list at 80, which made the page short by hiding the data.
`total` is sent so the page can say how many more there are rather than guess.
Static facts the page needs to build its controls without hardcoding them.

schema.title: Response Read Limits Api V1 Wishes Limits Get

ActionNode.title: ActionNode
ActionNode.description: One action by one character — what a `RotationStep` was.

ActionOffer.title: ActionOffer
ActionOffer.description:
One move a particular character can be given, as a button can draw it.

**Composed here rather than assembled by the client**, for the reason `/options` exists at
all: the correspondence between gcsim's actions and the catalogue's talents is one thing
(`gcsim_keys`) and it should have one owner.

Amplifying.title: Amplifying
Amplifying.description:
The four amplifying reactions, by *which element triggers*.

The multiplier depends on the triggering element, not on the pair. Sources, both at the
pin: `pkg/reactable/melt.go` (Pyro onto Cryo → 2.0; Cryo onto Pyro → 1.5) and
`pkg/reactable/vaporize.go` (Hydro onto Pyro → 2.0; Pyro onto Hydro → 1.5).

Transformative and additive reactions are **not** here: the BRIEF's ship order puts them
after the gauge engine, and gcsim computes them on a different path entirely
(`calcDirectReaction`, with its own `6*em/(2000+em)` bonus). Adding them to this enum
would invite them into a chain that cannot express them.

ArtifactEquip.title: ArtifactEquip
ArtifactEquip.description:
Body for `PATCH /artifacts/{id}` — the equip binding, and nothing else.

**Only `build_id`.** An artifact's stats come from the GOOD import, with `main_stat_value`
*derived* from the committed value table for its rarity, level and main stat rather than
read off a screen. A patch that accepted `level` or `main_stat_value` would let the one
number this repo derives be overwritten by hand, and every later use of that piece would
be a confident calculation over a figure a user typed.

`None` means unequip, and is not the same as omitting the field — which
`extra="forbid"` plus a required `build_id` makes impossible to confuse.

ArtifactOptions.title: ArtifactOptions
ArtifactOptions.description:
The vocabulary an inventory needs to draw a row.

Published **once** rather than decorated onto every artifact: 26 stats and 5 slots
repeated across 800 pieces is the same table 800 times. The same reasoning as
`/rotations/options`, arrived at from the other direction — there the risk was a client
list drifting from the validator, here it is a client list existing at all.

substat_analysis.title: Substat Analysis
substat_analysis.description:
What each substat is made of, positionally aligned with `substats`.

Genshin publishes no roll count — a substat is a *sum* — so it is reconstructed by
decomposing the total over the values the stat can roll. Over a real 2,370-artifact
export, 85.0% of substats decompose exactly one way (every roll value known), 10.2%
more admit several decompositions that agree on the count, and 4.8% match nothing.

**Ambiguity is reported, never smoothed.** `rolls` is null where the decompositions
disagree on how many there were, and `roll_tiers` is null unless exactly one fits.
`roll_value` needs no decomposition and is therefore present on almost every line —
it is the total as a multiple of one best-case roll, and the number that actually
answers "is this line any good".

A parallel list rather than keys inside `substats`, because `substats` is a JSONB
column with no schema behind it: rows written by an older importer are still valid
and must not be rewritten to carry fields they never had.

potential.description:
A.5/G.9 — how much upgrading this piece has left.

**Null when the schedule cannot answer for this piece**: a rarity it does not cover,
or a level that rarity cannot reach. Null rather than raising, because one impossible
row must not take down a list of eight hundred — the failure the inventory page met
from the other side. And null rather than zero, because zero is the honest answer for
a maxed piece, so collapsing the two would hide the broken row behind a plausible
number.

Computed here rather than on the model: `app/models` importing `app/services` is the
wrong way round, and this needs nothing the row does not already carry.

ArtifactSetRead.title: ArtifactSetRead
ArtifactSetRead.description:
One artifact set and its affixes.

`piece_thresholds` is **data**, not the constant `[2, 4]`: 60 of the 65 sets at 7.0.51
are `[2, 4]` and five are `[1]` — the "Prayers" circlets. A client hardcoding 2pc/4pc
gets those five wrong, which is why the field is on the summary and not buried.

ArtifactSlot.title: ArtifactSlot
ArtifactSlot.description:
The five artifact slots, keyed by the source's internal names.

Source: the `parts` keys of an artifact *detail* payload
(`gi/7.0.51/en/artifact/15025.json`, committed under `tests/fixtures/nanoka_gi/detail/`).

A `StrEnum` and not an `IntEnum`, per DESIGN §3: Genshin's slots are named rather than
ordered, and the fixed-main-stat property of flower and plume belongs in a
slot-to-allowed-mains table (C.5), not in the ordering of an enum.

Member names are the community/display terms; **values are the payload's keys**, which
is what the importer matches on.

AscensionPassiveRead.title: AscensionPassiveRead
AscensionPassiveRead.description:
One ascension passive.

`unlock_ascension` is **nullable and stays that way**: a passive gated by a condition
rather than a phase has no phase, and a `0` there would claim it is ungated.

AvailableHitRead.title: AvailableHitRead
AvailableHitRead.description:
One hit a build can be asked about, in the terms `HitSpec.talent` takes.

Offered from the **same parse** `resolve_talent_hit` uses, so a page built from this
cannot name a hit the resolver then refuses — the picker-matches-validator guarantee this
repo applies wherever a user chooses from a list.

AvatarRead.title: AvatarRead
AvatarRead.description:
The character standing in for an account, as the client needs it to draw one.

**One optional object rather than three flat nullable fields.** `avatar_character_id`,
`avatar_name` and `avatar_icon` side by side are three things that can disagree; this is
either present or it is not.

`name` is here because the client needs it for the image's `alt` text and for the line
naming who is shown — and a bare id would make the account page fetch the whole catalogue
before it could name what it is already displaying. `icon` may still be null: it is a
seeding gap for a handful of rows, and `CatalogueIcon` renders nothing at all for one.

BannerKind.title: BannerKind
BannerKind.description: Which limited banner is being planned for.

Binary.title: Binary
Binary.description: `a && b`, `.x.energy >= 30`. Two operands and an operator with a precedence.

BranchNode.title: BranchNode
BranchNode.description:
An `if` / `else if` / `else` chain, as **one** node.

gcsim evaluates the chain once and takes one arm. Modelling it as separate `if`s would
re-test each condition after the previous arm ran, and an action inside an arm can change
what the next one tests — `internal/characters/flins/skill.go:56` deletes the very status
its block is guarded on. `DESIGN_conditional_steps.md` records that hazard; this closes
**OQ-C3** by giving the `else` somewhere to live.

BuildCreate.title: BuildCreate
BuildCreate.description:
Body for `POST /builds`.

Unknown fields are refused rather than dropped, for the reason `BuildUpdate` records: a
typo'd field name silently becomes "you did not set that", and the caller is told the
write succeeded.

BuildImportSummary.title: BuildImportSummary
BuildImportSummary.description: What reconstituting builds from the export did, and did not do.

BuildOption.title: BuildOption
BuildOption.description:
A build the user could read a starting state from.

**A build may be hypothetical** — this app lets you gear a character you do not own — so
the planner names which build it read and shows the levels it took, rather than quietly
treating a scenario as the account's truth.

BuildOptions.title: BuildOptions
BuildOptions.description:
What an editor may offer for a build.

The same guarantee `/rotations/options` gives (R.5): **the form offers exactly what the
validator accepts.** `talents` is `LEVELLED_TALENTS`, which is both what `_validated_talents`
checks against and what `gcsim_config._talents` renders — so a form built from this cannot
produce a key that is stored and ignored, or one that renders as level 1.

A list rather than a TypeScript union, because a generated type is erased at runtime and a
page needs to *iterate* these to draw three inputs. Hardcoding them there would be a third
copy of the tuple.

BuildPriorityOrder.title: BuildPriorityOrder
BuildPriorityOrder.description:
Body for `PUT /builds/priority` — the ranking, in order, as build ids.

**The whole order at once, rather than a priority per `PATCH`.** A ranking is a
permutation: setting one build's rank without the others produces ties and gaps, and a
drag-and-drop list sends the finished order anyway. One request also means one transaction,
so a half-applied reorder is not a state anyone can observe.

weapon_display.title: Weapon Display
weapon_display.description:
`Freedom-Sworn · R1 · Lv90` — the weapon as a build actually holds it.

Published rather than left to each client for the same reason `weapon_type_display`
is. Three surfaces named a build's weapon — the saved list, the team slot picker and
the optimize header — and all three printed the bare name, so a character showed
`C6` while the weapon beside it showed nothing about how far it had been taken. Three
format strings would have been three chances to disagree about a build's own gear.

`None` when there is no weapon: `weapon_id` is nullable by design (OQ-T3), and a
caller should render "no weapon" rather than a level for a weapon that is not there.

Refinement before level because refinement is the scarcer fact — a Lv90 R1 and a Lv90
R5 are different weapons in practice, and the R is what a reader is scanning for.

BuildUpdate.title: BuildUpdate
BuildUpdate.description:
Body for `PATCH /builds/{id}` — all fields optional.

`character_id` is **not** here, and an unknown field is now a 422 rather than silently
dropped (T.1). Those two facts go together: sending `{"character_id": …}` used to return
200 having changed nothing, so a caller was told their edit succeeded when it had been
discarded. Changing a build's character makes it a different build — and
`uq_builds_owner_character` would collide with the existing one anyway — so the field
stays out, and refusing it says so instead of pretending.

CalibrationConfigs.title: CalibrationConfigs
CalibrationConfigs.description:
The two configs a recipe is built from.

The browser runs both through `sample()`: the first becomes the recipe, and the difference
between them identifies what each frozen term was converted from.

CalibrationRequest.title: CalibrationRequest
CalibrationRequest.description:
Body for `POST /builds/{id}/calibrate` (R.3).

One calibration per **4-piece state**. `RESEARCH_conditional_sets.md`: every 4-piece bonus
in the game is conditional, so only a run with the set equipped can hold it — and R.2
measured the cost of not doing so at **15–25 % understated**.

CallNode.title: CallNode
CallNode.description: `f(a, b);` — a call to a user-defined function.

weapon_type_display.title: Weapon Type Display
weapon_type_display.description:
`Sword`, beside the raw `WEAPON_SWORD_ONE_HAND`.

The value is the game's internal spelling — the reason `Element` reads well in this
output and `WeaponType` does not. Published rather than left to each client, because
a page deriving it would be a second copy of `WeaponType.display`.

weapon_type_icon.title: Weapon Type Icon
weapon_type_icon.description:
The class mark's basename — Genshin's own sword/bow/polearm/claymore/catalyst glyph.

On the **mixin**, so a character card and a weapon card cannot show different marks
for the same class. They spell the class differently in the source
(`WEAPON_CROSSBOW` against `ITEM_TPS_WEAPON`) and this is the second thing after
`weapon_type_display` that would otherwise be derived twice.

`None` for the crossbow class, which has no mark at this pin — two unreleased Traveler
variants with no talents seeded, so there is nothing to derive.
`app/services/weapon_symbols.py` on why the mapping is a query and not five lines
written from memory.

element_icon.title: Element Icon
element_icon.description:
The vision emblem's basename — the flame, the droplet, the snowflake.

Published rather than derived client-side, for the same reason `weapon_type_icon` is:
a page building `f"{element}.webp"` would request art nobody vendored the moment a
patch adds a vision, and would render a broken mark instead of nothing.

`None` for the two rows whose element is the literal `"None"`.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description:
The name to put on a card, which for sixteen characters is not `name`.

Every `Traveler` row is *named* `Traveler` — no gender column, no title, and upstream
publishes one `en` value for all sixteen. So the roster tab drew Aether Pyro and Lumine
Pyro as the same row twice, and the two unreleased bodies, which have no element and so
no chip, drew *identically*.

**Computed rather than stored**, like `element_icon` and `stars` beside it: a display
name is presentation, and storing it would mean a migration whenever a body or element
is added plus a second copy of the truth to keep in step.

`app/services/traveler.py` says why it is keyed on the icon — it is the only signal
that exists — and `docs/RESEARCH_traveler_identity.md` has the rest.

stars.title: Stars
stars.description:
`5` for `five_star`, from `Rarity.stars`.

Published for the same reason `WeaponSummary.stars` is: the characters page was
deriving it with `rarity === 'five_star' ? 5 : 4`, which silently calls anything else
— a lower rarity, a null — a four-star. A second copy of a rule that already exists
server-side, and the copy is the one that guesses.
