CharacterSummary.title: CharacterSummary
CharacterSummary.description: A character as a list entry.

CharacterWeaponGuideRead.title: CharacterWeaponGuideRead
CharacterWeaponGuideRead.description:
A character's captured recommendations, and where they came from.

**The citation travels with the claim.** `url` and `retrieved_at` are published so a reader
can open the page rather than take this repo's word — the same discipline as the reaction
table, and for the reason `CLAUDE.md` names: fabricated citations in curated data is the
failure this project must not import.

CompareWeaponsResponse.title: CompareWeaponsResponse
CompareWeaponsResponse.description: Every candidate scored in one build, best first — and what the ranking cannot see.

ContextKeyRead.title: ContextKeyRead
ContextKeyRead.description:
The cache key for a rotation, and the parts it was computed from.

The parts are returned because a key is a hash: opaque by design, and impossible to
check by eye. A caller that gets an unexpected cache miss can see *what was hashed*
rather than guess, which is the difference between a debuggable key and a magic one.

ContributionRead.title: ContributionRead
ContributionRead.description: One value and where it came from.

CraftingBonusRead.title: CraftingBonusRead
CraftingBonusRead.description: A character whose passive changes what crafting costs.

DeclaredFunction.title: DeclaredFunction
DeclaredFunction.description: One `fn` a rotation declares, as the builder needs to offer it.

Diagnostic.title: Diagnostic
Diagnostic.description: One problem, with the position an editor underlines.

DivergenceRead.title: DivergenceRead
DivergenceRead.description:
How much substituting a neighbouring bucket appears to cost, and the noise under it.

Both numbers, never one verdict. `docs/RESEARCH_er_bucketing.md` records the significance
test that flagged a bucket where no context change was possible — burst casts are
discrete, so per-iteration DPS is a multi-modal mixture and `sd/√n` understates it. A test
that misfired on its first dataset is not a test to hide a number behind.

DrawModel.title: DrawModel
DrawModel.description:
Everything a projection needs that is the same for every piece.

Sent once on the snapshot. Per piece it would be 2,370 copies of two small tables.

Element.title: Element
Element.description:
The seven visions.

Source: distinct `element` values in `gi/7.0.51/character.json` — `Anemo`, `Cryo`,
`Dendro`, `Electro`, `Geo`, `Hydro`, `Pyro`, plus a literal `"None"` carried by two
characters (the Traveler entries), which is **handled by `parse`, not mapped**.

**Physical is deliberately absent.** It is a damage type, not a vision; modelling it as
a peer of the seven is the ZZZ-shaped trap DESIGN §2.6 calls out by name. See
`DamageType`.

ElementRead.title: ElementRead
ElementRead.description:
One vision, and the emblem that stands for it.

Published rather than derived client-side, for exactly the reason `element_icon` is: a
filter bar building `f"{element}.webp"` would request art nobody vendored the moment a
patch adds an eighth vision, and would render a broken mark instead of nothing. The
allowlist lives in `app/services/element_symbols.py` and this is its only other reader.

**Physical is not a vision** and is absent, which is the ZZZ-shaped trap DESIGN §2.6 names.

EnemyProfileRead.title: EnemyProfileRead
EnemyProfileRead.description:
One enemy profile.

**`base_hp` / `base_atk` / `base_def` are curve bases, not level-90 stats.** A
Hilichurl's `base_hp` is `13.584`. The number a damage calculation needs is that base
scaled by the growth curve named in `stat_curves` at `level`. Anything that multiplies
these by a crit multiplier and calls the result damage is wrong, so `stat_curves` ships
with them and the field names keep the word "base".

`level` describes what the profile is *for*; it is not a level these stats have been
evaluated at.

EnemySpec.title: EnemySpec
EnemySpec.description:
The target.

`Enemy` requires **all eight** damage channels, because treating a missing one as 0%
overstates every hit against it. Listing eight numbers on every request is not something
to ask of a caller, so any channel `resistances` does not mention takes
`default_resistance` — a **stated** default that appears in the schema and can be
changed, rather than a silent zero.

That distinction is the whole point: the first version of this documented a 10% default
and passed `{}` straight through, so every request without an explicit eight-channel map
was a 500 from inside the damage chain.

EquippedStatsRead.title: EquippedStatsRead
EquippedStatsRead.description:
One build's equipped artifacts, summed into the kernel's own quantities.

**Narrow on purpose.** The browser already has a translation-free path to *every* artifact
via `/artifacts/inventory`, and widening that payload with a build binding would be paid
for across a 2,370-piece inventory to answer a question about five pieces. This is the five.

Summed rather than listed, because every consumer wants the total: `evaluateRecipe` takes
one number per quantity, and a caller re-summing five pools is a second place for the
vocabulary to be got wrong.

The translation is `stat_calculator._quantity_for_prop`, the same one `/artifacts/inventory`
uses — which is the reason this is computed here rather than in TypeScript. A client-side
mapping would be a second definition of what every stat means, with a silent failure mode: a
mis-mapped substat produces a build optimal for a stat the character does not have.

ExpBillRead.title: ExpBillRead
ExpBillRead.description: The EXP half of levelling. `mora` is null while the divisor is uncurated — not zero.

ExpBookRead.title: ExpBookRead
ExpBookRead.description:
One EXP denomination and how many of it the shortfall needs.

Carries its own name and icon because these are **not** material rows: EXP is a pool that
`exp_bill` has already netted against stock, so listing them in the materials table
subtracted the same stock twice. They are rendered from the EXP line instead, and need
their own art to do it.

ExplainRequest.title: ExplainRequest
ExplainRequest.description:
Body for `POST /builds/{id}/explain`.

**No contributions in the body, deliberately.** The caller names artifacts by id and the
server resolves them through the same `build_combination_log` the search and the ranker
use. Accepting numbers from the client would make the explanation an account of whatever
was posted rather than of the build, and an explanation of a lie is the one output where
that would be hardest to notice.

ExplainResponse.title: ExplainResponse
ExplainResponse.description: A build's account of itself, and optionally of what it improves on.

FnNode.title: FnNode
FnNode.description:
`fn name(params) { body }`.

Structural here, and **authored as text** — owner, 2026-09-03: *"user defined functions
almost need to be written… they'll have to author them themselves."* Measured: of the 41
corpus configs defining one, 41 have control flow in the body and 30 take a parameter, so
there is no simple-function case a form could have covered.

GcsimCandidateConfig.title: GcsimCandidateConfig
GcsimCandidateConfig.description: One candidate, and the config that simulates it.

GcsimComparisonConfigs.title: GcsimComparisonConfigs
GcsimComparisonConfigs.description:
What the browser needs to run a gcsim weapon comparison.

**The server emits configs; it does not simulate.** `RESEARCH_gcsim_embed.md` §6 put gcsim
in the browser, and W.4 measured a full sword pool at ~96 s across four workers — that is
a job on the user's machine, not a request a server should hold open.

GcsimComparisonRequest.title: GcsimComparisonRequest
GcsimComparisonRequest.description:
Body for `POST /builds/{id}/compare-weapons/gcsim` (W.6).

**`rotation_id` is required and has no default.** A rotation belongs to a *team*, and a
build can sit in several teams each with several rotations, so there is no rotation this
endpoint could pick on its own. Inventing one would make the ranking an answer about a
rotation the user never wrote — which is the same objection that closed Chunk I's
optimization half.

GoodImportRequest.title: GoodImportRequest
GoodImportRequest.description:
Body for `POST /artifacts/import/good`.

`mode` has **no default**, and that is the point. GOOD carries no stable per-artifact
identifier, so `append` run twice duplicates a whole inventory — and a duplicated goblet
is not clutter, it is a search that will happily recommend wearing the same piece twice.
`replace` deletes. Neither is safe to reach by omission, so the request states which.

GoodImportResponse.title: GoodImportResponse
GoodImportResponse.description:
What the import did.

`rejected` lists both the artifacts the parser refused and the ones whose set this
database does not know. A caller showing a user what happened should not have to tell
those apart, and a partial import that reported only a count would be the thing this
importer exists not to be.

HistogramBinRead.title: HistogramBinRead
HistogramBinRead.description: One bar of the resin distribution: `[low, high)` holding `probability`.

HitSpec.title: HitSpec
HitSpec.description:
The hit a search or a ranking is judged on.

**Either a `multiplier` or a `talent`, never both and never neither.** Naming the talent
resolves the multiplier from the build's own character at its own talent level; giving a
multiplier outright still works, because asking about a hypothetical hit is legitimate and
the optimizer's fixtures do exactly that.

**`channel` stays required either way.** The published table gives a multiplier and says
nothing about which element the hit lands as — a normal attack is physical for most
characters and not for a catalyst user, and infusions move it. Deriving it would be
inventing a rule the data does not state.

Identifier.title: Identifier
Identifier.description: The config's own variable — a loop index, a `let` binding, a function parameter.

ImportRejection.title: ImportRejection
ImportRejection.description: One artifact that did not make it in, and why.

InventorySnapshot.title: InventorySnapshot
InventorySnapshot.description:
Every owned artifact in one response, plus the version that identifies it.

**OQ-S3, answered: the browser holds the inventory and revalidates it.** The transfer is
not the deciding factor — a 2,000-piece account is ~936 KB of JSON, ~234 KB gzipped, so
fetching per search and holding across searches cost about the same. What differs is
**staleness**: an inventory held across a GOOD re-import is an inventory containing
artifacts the user no longer owns, and a search over it would recommend wearing them.

So the payload carries a `version` and the route serves `304 Not Modified` against
`If-None-Match`. The browser keeps the pieces and asks a cheap question before each
search, which is the correctness of fetching at the cost of holding.

Paging is deliberately not offered here. `GET /artifacts` pages for a UI list; a search
needs the whole inventory at one instant, and four paged round-trips have no such
instant — a concurrent import shifts every offset under the reader.

KernelCandidate.title: KernelCandidate
KernelCandidate.description:
One artifact, as `search.ts`'s `Candidate` reads it.

O.2. Smaller than `ArtifactRead` and translated: `stats` is keyed by **kernel quantity**,
with the main stat and every substat summed into one map, because the kernel takes one
number per quantity.

The translation is `stat_calculator._quantity_for_prop`, which decides what every stat
means and refuses rather than guessing. Doing it in TypeScript would be a second
definition of the vocabulary with a silent failure mode — a mis-mapped substat produces a
build optimal for a stat the character does not have, presented as the answer.

KernelHit.title: KernelHit
KernelHit.description: The hit, resolved. `search.ts`'s `Hit` in its own spelling.

KernelSetBonus.title: KernelSetBonus
KernelSetBonus.description: One tier of one set, in the terms the browser kernel reads.

LibraryRotationRead.title: LibraryRotationRead
LibraryRotationRead.description:
One published rotation, as the library lists it.

**Not `RotationRead` with fields added.** That schema is what an author sees of their own
rotation; this is what a stranger sees of someone else's, and the difference is the point:
`like_count` and `liked_by_me` are facts about the *caller*, and `characters` is the
derived index rather than the steps.

The steps are here too, because a rotation nobody can read before copying is one nobody
should copy — the whole argument for `POST /{id}/compile` applies to a shared rotation with
more force.

Literal.title: Literal
Literal.description: A number, a boolean, or a string.

LoginResponse.title: LoginResponse
LoginResponse.description: Response for `POST /auth/login` — bearer token and its expiry.

LoopNode.title: LoopNode
LoopNode.description: A `for` with a bound, or a `while` with a guard.

MaterialStockList.title: MaterialStockList
MaterialStockList.description:
Every material, owned first. **Unpaginated on purpose.**

The table holds ~514 rows, which is one ~40 KB response against a paging protocol and a
round trip per keystroke. It lists everything, including the handful no cost bill reaches:
a list that quietly omits the material a user is looking at is the bug this surface exists
to fix, wearing a different hat.

MaterialStockPatch.title: MaterialStockPatch
MaterialStockPatch.description:
The rows to change, **and only those**.

A list of named objects rather than a `dict[int, int]`, for the reason `ExpBookRead`
records. Partial by construction: a whole-inventory `PUT` built from a *filtered* view
would delete every material the filter was hiding, and this body cannot express that.

MaterialStockPatched.title: MaterialStockPatched
MaterialStockPatched.description:
What the write left behind: the rows it touched, and the balance as it now stands.

**The rows, not the whole inventory** — a `PATCH` names what it changes, and so does its
answer. `mora` is echoed whether or not this call set it, because the caller that did set
it needs to see the stored value rather than trust the one it sent.

MaterialStockRead.title: MaterialStockRead
MaterialStockRead.description: One material and how many of it this account holds.

MaterialStockUpdate.title: MaterialStockUpdate
MaterialStockUpdate.description:
One correction.

`count` is bounded **by the column** — `user_materials.count` is `int4` — and not by any
claim about the game's own stack limit, which this repository has not sourced. The bound
lives here as well as in the service so the refusal is in the published contract, and the
service keeps its own copy because a route is not the only possible caller.

MeResponse.title: MeResponse
MeResponse.description: Response for `GET /auth/me` — the current user's identity and account status.

MoraRead.title: MoraRead
MoraRead.description: The plan's mora, and the shortfall when the user has said what they hold.

OptimizationRunCreate.title: OptimizationRunCreate
OptimizationRunCreate.description: Body for `POST /optimization-runs` — a search the client has just finished.

OptimizationRunSummary.title: OptimizationRunSummary
OptimizationRunSummary.description: One row of the list — enough to choose between runs without loading any of them.

OptimizationRunUpdate.title: OptimizationRunUpdate
OptimizationRunUpdate.description:
Body for `PATCH /optimization-runs/{id}` — the two things a user changes afterwards.

Not the result. A saved run records what happened, and editing that would make the
library a place where numbers are asserted rather than measured.

OwnedWeaponOption.title: OwnedWeaponOption
OwnedWeaponOption.description: One physical copy the user owns. Duplicates are separate rows, as the game has them.

OwnedWeaponRead.title: OwnedWeaponRead
OwnedWeaponRead.description:
One weapon a user owns, with who is holding it.

**The holder is a portrait, not a name**, which is what the owner asked for — so this
publishes `holder_icon` beside `holder_name`. Both: an icon alone is a label only for
someone who already recognises the art, which is the argument `ElementChip` and
`WeaponMark` both make.

PlanRequest.title: PlanRequest
PlanRequest.description: One character, optionally one weapon, and where each should end up.

PlannerOptions.title: PlannerOptions
PlannerOptions.description: Everything the page needs to build a request.

ProgressIn.title: ProgressIn
ProgressIn.description: A level and an ascension phase. They move independently.

ProjectionInputs.title: ProjectionInputs
ProjectionInputs.description:
What the client needs to project one piece forward to its maximum level.

`TASKS_artifact_ranking.md` A.4. The projection itself lives in `sim/artifact-projection.ts`,
next to the evaluator that consumes it; this is only the per-piece half of its input. The
parts shared by every piece — the roll ladders and the draw weights — ride on
`InventorySnapshot` once rather than 2,370 times.

**`substat_quantities` exists because `KernelCandidate.stats` cannot answer it.** That map
is summed, so a CRIT DMG circlet carrying a CRIT DMG substat is indistinguishable from one
that does not, and "which lines does this piece have" is exactly what decides whether an
upgrade deepens a line or creates one.

**Nothing here is a decomposition of the rolls the piece has already had.** That was the
first draft's assumption and it was wrong: projecting *future* rolls needs the line count
and the schedule, both exact, and never the history. `substat_rolls`' 85/11.5/3.5 exact /
estimated / unknown split governs the roll bars on the inventory card and does not reach
this. Recorded because `DESIGN_artifact_ranking.md` §6 names an undecomposable piece as a
reason to refuse a score, and for the projection it is not one.

Rarity.title: Rarity
Rarity.description:
Star rating, normalised across the two encodings the source uses.

Characters carry `rank` as a `QUALITY_*` string; weapons carry it as an integer 1-5, and
weapon *detail* payloads call the same thing `rarity`. `parse` accepts all of them.

`QUALITY_ORANGE_SP` is 5-star. It is **not** a one-off: 15 of the 150 characters carry
it, against DESIGN §2.6's "Aloy-class special" reading. Whether the SP distinction
matters to anything downstream is a Chunk D question; it does not change the star count.

RarityVocabularyEntry.title: RarityVocabularyEntry
RarityVocabularyEntry.description: One rarity, as a page needs to render it.

RawNode.title: RawNode
RawNode.description:
Source this parser did not model, carried exactly.

**The piece the whole design rests on.** Import reaches 100 % at the parser's first phase
because anything unmodelled becomes one of these, emits byte-identically, and blocks
nothing.

Two rules keep it from being silent degradation:

- **`reason` is required.** A user must be able to see *which* construct is carried rather
  than understood, because that is the difference between editing it in the builder and
  editing it as text.
- **It is opaque, never partial.** A production that cannot complete raws its *whole*
  construct. Reading half a `for` and raw-ing the body would produce a tree that looks
  structured and emits something the author did not write.

ReactionRead.title: ReactionRead
ReactionRead.description:
One elemental reaction, and what a party must field to produce it.

Published so the client filters on the **same committed table** the backend reads, rather
than a second copy that would drift — the reason every vocabulary here is served rather
than restated.

**Fifteen are listed and six are not** — Shattered, which is not an element pair, and the
five Lunar/Stellar variants by owner ruling (`DECISIONS.md` §23).
`app/services/reactions.py` explains each, and every excluded row stays in the committed
JSON with its citation. A filter that quietly mis-classified a team is worse than one that
offers less.

RefusedCandidate.title: RefusedCandidate
RefusedCandidate.description:
A candidate that could not be turned into a config, and why.

**Reported, never dropped.** A silently omitted candidate is a ranking that is missing a
weapon the user asked about, presented as though it had considered it — and the omission
is invisible precisely because the result still looks like a complete answer.

RegisterResponse.title: RegisterResponse
RegisterResponse.description: Response for `POST /auth/register` — always pending until email verification.

ResendVerificationResponse.title: ResendVerificationResponse
ResendVerificationResponse.description:
Response for `POST /auth/resend-verification` — identical for every address.

Answering differently for a known and an unknown address would make this endpoint the
account-enumeration oracle that `register` just stopped being.

ResinEstimateRead.title: ResinEstimateRead
ResinEstimateRead.description: Expected resin for one material, and the tier it is actually farmed at.

ResinTotalRead.title: ResinTotalRead
ResinTotalRead.description: A section's resin: the average, the shape, and everything with no number.

RetrievalOutcome.title: RetrievalOutcome
RetrievalOutcome.description:
What retrieval found, **or did not** — always a 200, never a 404.

DESIGN §3.5: *"A search can still arrive with no cached context. That must be a stated
outcome, not a silent fallback: simulate it now (a second or two), or say so. It must
never be to retrieve a distant neighbour and report its score as though it were close."*

A 404 would be the wrong shape for the second half of that. "Nothing close enough is
cached" is an **answer** — the caller acts on it by simulating — and dressing it as an
error invites the two reflexes an error provokes: retry it, or catch it and carry on with
whatever value was already in hand. The first wastes a round trip; the second is the
silent fallback this rule exists to forbid.

So the outcome is always 200 and `retrieved` is either present or explicitly null with a
reason beside it. A client cannot read this response and fail to notice which it got.

RetrievalRead.title: RetrievalRead
RetrievalRead.description: A run, and everything needed to judge whether it should have been used.

RollLadder.title: RollLadder
RollLadder.description: The values one substat can roll, at one rarity.

RosterCharacter.title: RosterCharacter
RosterCharacter.description: One character an editor may name in a step.

RosterEntryRead.title: RosterEntryRead
RosterEntryRead.description: One catalogue character and this user's answer about them.

owned.title: Owned
owned.description: Does this account have this character?

constellation.title: Constellation
constellation.description: Constellation 0-6. **Null means 'nobody has said', not C0** — the same three-state rule `owned` follows, because an unknown constellation and a zero one lead to different answers and only one of them is a claim. Omitting the field leaves any stored value alone; sending null clears it.

RosterRead.title: RosterRead
RosterRead.description: The whole roster in one response.

RotationCopyRequest.title: RotationCopyRequest
RotationCopyRequest.description: Body for `POST /rotations/{id}/copy` — which of the caller's teams to copy it onto.

RotationImportLinkRequest.title: RotationImportLinkRequest
RotationImportLinkRequest.description:
Body for `POST /rotations/import/link` — a gcsim database link instead of its config.

The owner asked for this because copying a config out of gcsim's viewer is the tedious
half of importing someone else's rotation.

**A link, parsed server-side into an id.** `gcsim_share` builds the URL it fetches from a
constant host, so nothing a user types ever reaches an HTTP client — see that module on
why a service that fetches a user-supplied URL is a request-forgery primitive.

RotationImportRead.title: RotationImportRead
RotationImportRead.description:
The steps a config was read as — a **preview**, not a saved rotation.

Importing does not create anything. The steps come back for the user to look at and then
save through the ordinary create endpoint, because a config that parses is not
automatically a rotation someone wants: it may name a team member they meant to swap, or
be the third variant of something they already have. Writing it for them would make
"import" a verb with a side effect nobody asked for, and the undo is a delete.

RotationImportRequest.title: RotationImportRequest
RotationImportRequest.description: Body for `POST /rotations/import` — a gcsim config to read back into steps.

RotationOptions.title: RotationOptions
RotationOptions.description:
Everything an editor needs to offer a step that will be accepted.

Both halves come from the same place the write path reads: `actions` from
`authorable_actions()`, `teams` from the roster extraction `_check_steps_against_team`
validates against. The guarantee is **the picker offers exactly what the validator
accepts** — the alternative is a UI list that drifts, and a user told their own
selection is invalid.

RotationPreviewRequest.title: RotationPreviewRequest
RotationPreviewRequest.description:
Body for `POST /rotations/preview` — compile steps that have not been saved.

**Why this exists rather than the editor compiling client-side.** `POST /{id}/compile`
reads the *stored* rotation, so an editor showing a live preview of unsaved work would
either show the saved version — worse than no preview, because it looks current — or grow
a second compiler in TypeScript. The second compiler is the real hazard: the gates are what
stop gcsim's two silent failures (`DESIGN_rotation.md` §3.4), and two implementations of
them would eventually disagree about a config nobody reads.

So the steps come here and the **same** `compile_rotation` answers.

RotationSourceRead.title: RotationSourceRead
RotationSourceRead.description:
A parsed rotation, its diagnostics, and what it re-emits as.

**The tree is the source of truth and `source` is what it renders back to** (task 7.4).
A client that shows the returned `source` after an edit gets normalisation for free; one
that keeps the user's own text keeps their formatting. Both are valid, and the tree is the
same either way, which is the property that makes the two-way sync safe.

RotationSourceRequest.title: RotationSourceRequest
RotationSourceRequest.description:
Body for `POST /rotations/validate` — the source view's every keystroke.

Separate from `RotationImportRequest` because it means something different: an import is
a whole `.txt` file somebody else wrote, while this is the **rotation half** as the editor
holds it, sent back on change to be parsed and checked. Sharing one body would make the
two indistinguishable in a log and force the editor to fabricate a config wrapper.

RotationTree.title: RotationTree
RotationTree.description: A rotation, as an ordered tree.

RotationUpdate.title: RotationUpdate
RotationUpdate.description:
Body for `PATCH /rotations/{id}` — every field optional, partial update.

`team_id` is **not** here. Moving a rotation to another team would silently reinterpret
every step against a different party, and the steps that no longer resolve would be
discovered later, at compile time, far from the edit that caused it. Build a new rotation
for the other team.

ScalingStat.title: ScalingStat
ScalingStat.description:
What a talent's multiplier scales off.

gcsim's `UseHP` / `UseDef` / `UseEM` flags (`damage.go:52-62`), as data on the hit
rather than flags on a branch: a talent that scales off HP is a *described* talent, not
a special case in the chain (DESIGN §1 A6).

SearchContextRead.title: SearchContextRead
SearchContextRead.description:
Everything `search.ts`'s `SearchContext` needs except the inventory.

O.1. The inventory has its own home — `/artifacts/inventory`, which is ETag'd because the
browser holds it across searches (OQ-S3). This is the per-build, per-hit half.

**Published, not recomputed.** Every figure here is one the server already works out for
`/explain`: the base from `build_assembler.base_contributions`, set bonuses from the same
module, the hit through `resolve_talent_hit`. A second assembly of "what a build starts
from" is how two definitions of it begin — which `build_assembler` records having already
happened once.

`base` is keyed by **kernel quantity**, which is the reason this endpoint exists at all:
the kernel reads `base_atk` and the source spells it `FIGHT_PROP_BASE_ATTACK`, and the
mapping between them decides what every stat means.

SetAvatarRequest.title: SetAvatarRequest
SetAvatarRequest.description:
Body for `PUT /auth/me/avatar`.

`None` clears the avatar, so setting and unsetting are one code path with one shape — a
separate `DELETE` route would be a second path to keep honest for no gain.

**Required, and unknown fields are refused**, which for a nullable field is not
belt-and-braces. With a `None` default and Pydantic's `extra="ignore"`, a client sending
`{"characterId": "…"}` — one camelCase slip — validates, lands in the clear branch, and
**erases the avatar with a 200**. The handler's own docstring refuses to no-op on an
unknown id for a weaker version of this reason; here the 200 changed something nobody
asked to change. Both shapes are a 422 now. Same rule as `BuildCreate`.

SetEffectRead.title: SetEffectRead
SetEffectRead.description: A set bonus that applied, in the catalogue's own words.

SetRecommendationRead.title: SetRecommendationRead
SetRecommendationRead.description: One artifact set — or one *kind* of two-piece — KeqingMains lists for a character.

SimRunCoverage.title: SimRunCoverage
SimRunCoverage.description:
Which ER buckets this context already has, so a search knows what it must simulate.

Buckets rather than whole runs: the browser asks this before deciding how much work to
do, and shipping it every cached `result` to answer "how many" would make the cheap
question as expensive as the answer it is trying to avoid.

SimRunSubmit.title: SimRunSubmit
SimRunSubmit.description: One run the browser finished, offered to the cache.

SimulationNoteRead.title: SimulationNoteRead
SimulationNoteRead.description: What the retrieved run says, and how far it was from this build.

SlotVocabularyEntry.title: SlotVocabularyEntry
SlotVocabularyEntry.description: One artifact slot, as a page needs to render it.

StatAccountRead.title: StatAccountRead
StatAccountRead.description: One quantity and every contribution recorded against it.

StatDifferenceRead.title: StatDifferenceRead
StatDifferenceRead.description: One quantity that differs between the proposal and what is equipped.

StatVocabularyEntry.title: StatVocabularyEntry
StatVocabularyEntry.description: One stat, as a page needs to render it.

StatePath.title: StatePath
StatePath.description:
A reach into the simulation: `.furina.energy`, `.x.burst.ready`.

**Deliberately not an `Identifier`.** Only gcsim can answer one of these, and a condition
editor that treats both as "a string" ends up offering the loop index `i` as a character.

Strategy.title: Strategy
Strategy.description:
Which goal to reach first when one budget covers a character and their weapon.

After the primary goal the order is always *character to C0 → weapon to R1 → character to
C6 → weapon to R5*, which is the rule Fribbels' warp planner documents and the reason a
strategy is a single choice rather than a sortable list.

SubstatAnalysisRead.title: SubstatAnalysisRead
SubstatAnalysisRead.description: One substat's reconstruction. Every field is nullable, and the nulls are the point.

SwapNode.title: SwapNode
SwapNode.description: An explicit `x swap;`. gcsim also inserts one implicitly; this is the written kind.

TalentOption.title: TalentOption
TalentOption.description: One levelable talent. An alternate sprint has no cost ladder and is not offered.

TalentRead.title: TalentRead
TalentRead.description: One talent, with its per-level scaling table.

TalentRef.title: TalentRef
TalentRef.description:
Which hit of which talent, to be resolved against the build's own character.

This closed the chunk-H marker here. `HitSpec` used to require a bare `multiplier`,
because deriving one was the kit corpus's job and there is no kit corpus.
`talent_scaling` parses the published rows now, and M.4 checked that parse against gcsim
across 105 characters, so a caller can name the hit instead of typing 1.2091.

TalentScalingRead.title: TalentScalingRead
TalentScalingRead.description: One level's row of a talent's published multiplier table.

TalentTargetIn.title: TalentTargetIn
TalentTargetIn.description: Where one talent is and where it should end up.

TalentType.title: TalentType
TalentType.description:
What a character's `skills[]` entry actually is.

Source: the `promote["0"].icon` prefix in a character detail payload
(`gi/7.0.51/en/character/10000002.json`): `Skill_A_*` is the normal-attack talent,
`Skill_S_*` an elemental skill or an alternate sprint, `Skill_E_*` the burst.

**Never classify by list position.** Ayaka has four `skills[]` entries because she has
an alternate sprint; most characters have three. Positional indexing is a bug waiting
for the first character with a non-standard kit.

Telling an alternate sprint from an elemental skill needs more than the icon prefix —
both are `Skill_S_*`. That is D.3's problem, and `ALTERNATE_SPRINT` exists so D.3 has
somewhere to put the answer rather than inventing a member later.

TeamRoster.title: TeamRoster
TeamRoster.description: A team, and who is on it.

TeamUpdate.title: TeamUpdate
TeamUpdate.description: Body for `PATCH /teams/{id}` — all fields optional, partial update.

UncitedRead.title: UncitedRead
UncitedRead.description: Something the explanation could not attribute, reported rather than dropped.

UnmodelledPassiveRead.title: UnmodelledPassiveRead
UnmodelledPassiveRead.description: A passive stored in the catalogue that this comparison does not apply.

UnreadableArtifact.title: UnreadableArtifact
UnreadableArtifact.description:
A piece whose stats did not resolve, and why.

OQ-O2. Reported rather than dropped: a silently omitted piece is an inventory the user
cannot see is incomplete, and a search over it recommends the best of what it was *shown*
while looking like the best of what they own.

UpgradePotentialRead.title: UpgradePotentialRead
UpgradePotentialRead.description:
How much upgrading a piece has left, and the parts behind it.

The parts, not just a figure, because **a score is a claim** and this repo's standing rule
is that a number must be able to explain itself. "Potential: 3" is something a reader has
to take on trust; three rolls of a possible five, at +9 of a possible +20, is something
they can check.

The piece's own substats are **not** repeated here: `ArtifactRead` carries them in full,
with values and roll counts, so listing their names again would be the same answer in a
worse form. And which substat a roll enhances is not in the committed data at all — see
`app/services/artifact_potential.py`.

UserStatus.title: UserStatus
UserStatus.description: Admin-approval lifecycle state for a `User` account.

VerifyEmailRequest.title: VerifyEmailRequest
VerifyEmailRequest.description:
Body for `POST /auth/verify-email`.

**The token arrives in a POST body rather than a query string**, for two reasons and the
second is the one people miss. Secrets in URLs leak — into Referer headers, browser
history, nginx access logs and Cloudflare analytics — and a live account-takeover
credential should not be in an access log. And a `GET`-consumes endpoint is burned by the
mail scanners that fetch every link in an email before the human does: Outlook Safe Links,
corporate gateways, Slack unfurls. Against those, the scanner spends the single-use token
and the user's own click fails — a bug that reproduces only for users at companies you
cannot test against.

A scanner fetching the SPA route instead gets an HTML shell and does not execute Angular,
so the token survives to the real click. `DESIGN_open_registration.md` §2 (D-OR3).

VerifyEmailResponse.title: VerifyEmailResponse
VerifyEmailResponse.description:
Response for `POST /auth/verify-email`.

`session_token` is populated only when verification also approved the account, so the user
lands verified *and* signed in from one click with no password re-entry. That is the whole
UX win of this design and it costs one field.

Visibility.title: Visibility
Visibility.description:
Whether a rotation is the author's alone, or offered to everyone on this instance.

**Private is the default, and that is the decision** (`DECISIONS.md` §21, OQ-4). A private
rotation becoming visible by default is not a mistake that can be taken back — the author
cannot un-share what someone has already read — so sharing is something a user does, never
something that happens to them.

Two values, deliberately. A middle tier (unlisted, link-only, friends) is a permission
model, and this repo has no notion of one; adding a value here would be inventing the
smallest possible version of it and then owing the rest.

WaitNode.title: WaitNode
WaitNode.description: gcsim's `wait(n)` or `delay(n)` — 32 corpus configs use one.

WeaponClassRead.title: WeaponClassRead
WeaponClassRead.description:
One weapon class, its readable name, and its mark.

Published for the same reason `ElementRead` is: a filter bar otherwise carries its own
copy of the class list *and* builds an icon basename, and both are allowlists server-side
on purpose. `app/services/weapon_symbols.py` explains why the crossbow class is not here.

weapon_type_display.title: Weapon Type Display
weapon_type_display.description:
`Sword`, beside the raw `WEAPON_SWORD_ONE_HAND`.

The value is the game's internal spelling — the reason `Element` reads well in this
output and `WeaponType` does not. Published rather than left to each client, because
a page deriving it would be a second copy of `WeaponType.display`.

weapon_type_icon.title: Weapon Type Icon
weapon_type_icon.description:
The class mark's basename — Genshin's own sword/bow/polearm/claymore/catalyst glyph.

On the **mixin**, so a character card and a weapon card cannot show different marks
for the same class. They spell the class differently in the source
(`WEAPON_CROSSBOW` against `ITEM_TPS_WEAPON`) and this is the second thing after
`weapon_type_display` that would otherwise be derived twice.

`None` for the crossbow class, which has no mark at this pin — two unreleased Traveler
variants with no talents seeded, so there is nothing to derive.
`app/services/weapon_symbols.py` on why the mapping is a query and not five lines
written from memory.

sub_stat_display.title: Sub Stat Display
sub_stat_display.description:
`CRIT DMG` for `FIGHT_PROP_CRITICAL_HURT`, from `StatType.display`.

Published rather than left to the client, for the reason `weapon_type_display`
already is: a page translating `FIGHT_PROP_*` itself would be a second copy of a
rule that lives in `models/enums.py`, free to drift. The catalogue was printing the
raw key on screen because there was nothing else to print.

Null for the **18** weapons whose payload substat is absent — a weapon with no
substat, not one whose substat is unknown. (Counted, not copied: two comments in
`services/stat_calculator.py` say "ten" and "the eight TPS entries" for related but
differently-scoped sets, and repeating either here would have made a third number.)

stars.description: `5` for `five_star`. The card draws these; nobody reads `four_star`.

WeaponRead.description: A weapon in full, with its growth curves and refinement rows.

WeaponRecommendationRead.description: One weapon KeqingMains lists for a character.

sub_stat_display.title: Sub Stat Display
sub_stat_display.description:
`CRIT DMG` for `FIGHT_PROP_CRITICAL_HURT`, from `StatType.display`.

Published rather than left to the client, for the reason `weapon_type_display`
already is: a page translating `FIGHT_PROP_*` itself would be a second copy of a
rule that lives in `models/enums.py`, free to drift. The catalogue was printing the
raw key on screen because there was nothing else to print.

Null for the **18** weapons whose payload substat is absent — a weapon with no
substat, not one whose substat is unknown. (Counted, not copied: two comments in
`services/stat_calculator.py` say "ten" and "the eight TPS entries" for related but
differently-scoped sets, and repeating either here would have made a third number.)

stars.title: Stars
stars.description: `5` for `five_star`. The card draws these; nobody reads `four_star`.

WeaponSummary.title: WeaponSummary
WeaponSummary.description:
A weapon as a list entry.

`base_atk` and `sub_stat_type` are nullable because eight rows (the `ITEM_TPS_WEAPON`
family, ids 224001-224008) publish `atk: null` and `sub: null`. They are imported
visibly rather than dropped; a client should expect to see them.

WeaponType.title: WeaponType
WeaponType.description:
The six weapon classes.

Source: `character.json` `weapon` and `weapon.json` `type`. **The two indexes disagree
on the sixth.** Characters spell the crossbow class `WEAPON_CROSSBOW` (2 characters);
weapons spell it `ITEM_TPS_WEAPON` (8 weapons) and `WEAPON_CROSSBOW` appears nowhere in
`weapon.json`. Both spellings therefore map here, via `parse`.

DESIGN §2.6 recorded only `WEAPON_CROSSBOW`, having read the character index alone.

WishBannerList.title: WishBannerList
WishBannerList.description: Banners newest first, with how many there are in total.

WishBannerRead.title: WishBannerRead
WishBannerRead.description: One banner run, for the picker.

icon.title: Icon
icon.description: Catalogue basename, or null when the name does not resolve — a character newer than the pinned catalogue. **Null renders nothing rather than a broken image**, which is why banners store names and resolve here rather than storing ids.

WishFeaturedItem.title: WishFeaturedItem
WishFeaturedItem.description: A featured character or weapon, with whatever art the catalogue has for it.

WishHistogramBin.title: WishHistogramBin
WishHistogramBin.description: One bar of the exact distribution of wishes to a rung.

fetched_at.title: Fetched At
fetched_at.description: When the store last read the workbook. Present so a page can say how old these numbers are: stale projected income is the failure mode that goes wrong silently.

WishIncomeRead.title: WishIncomeRead
WishIncomeRead.description: The income table, and when it was last refreshed.

is_estimate.title: Is Estimate
is_estimate.description: The workbook's own `est.` marker — a forecast, not a settled total.

WishIncomeVersionRead.title: WishIncomeVersionRead
WishIncomeVersionRead.description: One game version's income at all three tiers.

label.title: Label
label.description: What a player calls this rung: "C3", "R2".

median_wishes.title: Median Wishes
median_wishes.description: Wishes at which the chance first reaches 50%, or null if it never does.

histogram.title: Histogram
histogram.description: The exact distribution of wishes needed, binned for drawing. **The population, not a sample** — no sampling error, identical on every run. Sent for the rungs the page can chart; empty on the rest to keep the payload small.

budget.title: Budget
budget.description: Wishes available: primogems/160 + fate + projected income.

wallet_wishes.title: Wallet Wishes
wallet_wishes.description: Wishes the wallet alone is worth, before refund.

refund_source.title: Refund Source
refund_source.description: `roster` when the refund was computed exactly from the account and the banner's featured 4-stars, `tier` when it came from the chosen constant.

refunded_wishes.title: Refunded Wishes
refunded_wishes.description: Wishes the starglitter refund adds. Zero when the tier is `none`.

published_worst_case.title: Published Worst Case
published_worst_case.description: The largest number of wishes HoYoverse advertises may be needed for one copy, for the plan's first banner. Published, NOT read off the fitted pity curve — the curve's far tail is not identified and would understate it.

WishPlanRead.title: WishPlanRead
WishPlanRead.description: The ladder, and the budget it was measured against.

character.description: Simple mode: the character to plan, with `weapon` and `strategy`.

weapon.description: Simple mode: their signature weapon, or null to plan alone.

strategy.description: Simple mode: which goal to reach first.

targets.title: Targets
targets.description: Custom mode: goals in spending order. Each needs `target_copies`.

banner_slug.title: Banner Slug
banner_slug.description: A banner from `/wishes/banners`. When given, the refund is computed **exactly** from its featured 4-stars and the caller's roster instead of from a tier.

starglitter_refund.title: Starglitter Refund
starglitter_refund.description: How much of the budget comes back as Masterless Starglitter: none, low (every 4-star a weapon), average (an even split), high (every 4-star a maxed character).

intertwined_fate.title: Intertwined Fate
intertwined_fate.description: Acquaint Fate is deliberately not accepted: it buys the standard banner.

extra_wishes.title: Extra Wishes
extra_wishes.description: Projected income the caller has opted into, in whole wishes.

WishPlanRequest.title: WishPlanRequest
WishPlanRequest.description:
A player's wallet, and either one character to plan or an explicit list of goals.

**Two shapes, one route.** `character` (plus an optional `weapon` and a `strategy`) is
Fribbels' Simple mode: the whole ladder for one character, ordered by the strategy.
`targets` is its Multi Target: an ordered list of goals across several characters,
spending the same budget down the list.

label.title: Label
label.description: What to call this target's rungs — a character name.

pity.title: Pity
pity.description: Wishes since the last 5-star on this banner.

guaranteed.title: Guaranteed
guaranteed.description: Whether the next 5-star is guaranteed to be the promotional item.

lost_fifty_fifties.title: Lost Fifty Fifties
lost_fifty_fifties.description: 50/50s lost since the last one WON — the Capturing Radiance counter. It is one account-wide counter, so only the FIRST target of a plan may set it.

owned_copies.title: Owned Copies
owned_copies.description: Copies already held. C2 is 3; R3 is 3.

target_copies.title: Target Copies
target_copies.description: Total copies to reach. Only used by a custom plan; a simple plan's goals come from its strategy.

WishTarget.title: WishTarget
WishTarget.description: One banner's starting position within a plan.
